package_info.package_versions: all published versions (since at least Dec 4, 2023)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages abuse the npm registry by storing and distributing large, non-software media files (movies, video clips, and eBooks), violating the platform's terms of service and threatening the integrity and hygiene of the software supply chain. While not containing traditional malware, their presence constitutes a supply chain risk, potential copyright violation, and can be leveraged for illicit content distribution.

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when package is downloaded or inspected; no code execution required)
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (multiple .ts files, e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts, etc.)
required_permissions: filesystem (to store and distribute large binary files)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Stores and delivers large video files (movie clips) as part of the package contents. These files are not referenced by any code and serve only as media payloads, not as software assets.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Software packages are expected to contain code and necessary assets, not large, unrelated media files. The presence of multi-gigabyte video files is highly anomalous and suggests abuse of the npm registry for non-software content distribution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal npm packages contain JavaScript/TypeScript code and small assets directly related to the software's function. The inclusion of split movie files with no code referencing them is a clear violation of platform norms.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate packages may include small demo videos or images for documentation, or media assets for open-source video players, but never full-length movies or pirated content, especially without any code utilizing them.
key_indicators: Multiple large .ts files (MPEG-TS video segments) in package root
Total package size approximately 54.5 MB per package, far exceeding typical npm package sizes
No actual code or software functionality present in the package
File names and structure consistent with split media distribution

execution_context.trigger: import-time (when package is downloaded or inspected; no code execution required)
execution_context.file_location: package root directory (JSON files, e.g., comments.json)
required_permissions: filesystem (to store and distribute large JSON files)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Contains time-synced user comments, likely scraped from online video streaming platforms, accompanying the video files. These files are not referenced by any code and serve only as ancillary media data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: JSON files with time-synced comments are not typical for npm packages, especially when not related to any code functionality. Their presence alongside pirated media files suggests the package is intended for illicit media distribution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal packages may include configuration or metadata JSON, but not user comment data for pirated media. The lack of any code referencing these files further indicates their illegitimate purpose.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use could be subtitle or comment files for open-source video players, but only when accompanied by code that uses them. In this context, their presence is solely for pirated media distribution.
key_indicators: JSON files (e.g., comments.json) with time-synced user comments
No code referencing or utilizing these JSON files
Large JSON files present in package root alongside media segments
Metadata structure consistent with scraped streaming platform data

attack_chain.action: Attacker uploads multiple npm packages with the 'wlwz-' prefix, each containing a segment of a pirated movie (as .ts files) and associated comment data (as JSON files).
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages are available for download from the npm registry, making the pirated content accessible to anyone.

attack_chain.action: User (or automated script) downloads all packages with the 'wlwz-' prefix, reconstructs the full movie from the .ts segments, and optionally uses the comment data from the JSON files.
attack_chain.leads_to: Distribution and consumption of pirated media via npm, bypassing traditional content controls and polluting the software supply chain.

behavioral_signatures: npm packages with no executable code, only large binary media files (e.g., .ts, .mp4)
Packages containing multiple large .ts files and/or large JSON files with time-synced user comments in the package root
Unusually large package sizes (e.g., >50 MB) with no software functionality or code dependencies
Packages with repeated naming patterns (e.g., 'wlwz-*') and no legitimate project metadata
file_indicators: *.ts files in package root directory (e.g., video1.ts, video2.ts, etc.)
comments.json or similar large JSON files with time-synced comments in package root
package.json with minimal or no code dependencies and no main entry point
Absence of JavaScript/TypeScript source files or any code referencing the media or JSON files
network_indicators: No direct network indicators; malicious activity is limited to package content and does not involve runtime network communication
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Flag npm packages that contain large binary files (e.g., .ts, .mp4) unrelated to software functionality, especially when package size exceeds typical thresholds (e.g., >50 MB) and there is no accompanying code. Look for packages with repeated naming patterns (such as 'wlwz-*'), and inspect for the presence of media files or unrelated JSON data in the package root. Automated scanning should check for the absence of code files, the presence of large media or comment files, and anomalous package size. Packages with no main entry point or code dependencies, but with large non-code assets, should be prioritized for review.
